restrain

/rih-STRAYN/ - rhymes with train · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Restrain means to hold something back and keep it under control.

Etiquette restrained the court more surely than any guard: dukes swallowed insults that would have emptied a tavern.

Worked Example

Watt's governor is two brass balls on a spinning spindle, and it tamed the factory age. When the engine races, the balls swing wide and their linkage narrows the steam valve; let the spin sag and they droop, opening it again. The engine is never fought and never stopped — it is held, moment by moment, to the speed the millwright chose, by a device with no opinion about steam.

Restrain is the exact word for what the governor does, because to restrain is to hold something back and keep it under control — control, not defeat, is the point. Repress, this unit's heavier verb, puts force on top of a thing until it stops moving; the governor wants the engine running, just never running away.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hold back: Hold back is the plain phrase for the same motion — the hand on the collar, the swallowed reply. Restrain does the same holding in a more formal register — handlers, marshals, and courts restrain — and it points at the aim: kept under control, not stopped for good.

rein in: To rein in is the rider's correction — even pressure on the reins that guides a thing still moving, spending, or talking too fast. Restraining can go further: a restrained dog or crowd may be held quite still. Reining in steers; restraint holds.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

release: opens the hand and lets it go where it will

liberate: sets it free for good, with ceremony

Where it sits · how much freedom of movement remains — steady → restrain → pin

steady vs. restrain: Steady is a far lighter hold than restrain — a hand on the shoulder, keeping balance without taking charge, while a restrained animal is genuinely held and cannot simply walk away.

pin vs. restrain: Pin goes further than restrain — a restrained animal can still shift and settle; a pinned one cannot move at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back

Root — strain

Root — strain: to draw tight (Latin stringere)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (back) + strain (to draw tight) = to draw back tight. Latin stringere is the binding root — cords, knots, tight grips — and restringere pulled the cord backward against whatever strained forward. Every modern use keeps that leash: the restrained thing is still pulling; the hold is still holding.

Use the root in a new word: strict

Use the root in a new word: strict: Strict is the same root as an adjective — rules drawn tight, with no slack left in them.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / protective

Restrain is the neutral hold: handlers restrain animals, marshals restrain crowds, and grown-ups restrain the urge to answer every message at midnight. It implies care as often as force. Repress is the same muscle turned political — the state on top of a strike; impede only slows a thing down; and to detain someone is to hold them in a place, not by the arm.
